extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who practice or seek to practice before the USPTO (patent and trademark practitioners), and parties interested in USPTO professional responsibility/discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing attorney conduct before the USPTO, especially fee handling, fee-sharing, disclosures, authorization to practice patent matters, and sanctions for violations under the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. §§10.xx and 11.xx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization to practice before the USPTO / unauthorized patent practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is not registered to practice before the Office in patent matters; as an attorney licensed in state bars he is authorized under 37 C.F.R. § 11.14(a) to practice before the USPTO in trademark or other non-patent matters and is subject to the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and Disciplinary Rules set forth at 37 C.F.R. § 10.20 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only registered patent practitioners may represent others before the USPTO in patent matters; attorneys not so registered may practice trademark/non-patent matters under §11.14(a) but remain subject to the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility. Unauthorized practice of patent matters by a non-registered person is impermissible and relevant to disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of retainer vs advance payment/security deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: A classic retainer is a sum paid to secure an attorney's availability and, if services are needed later, that retainer is not applied to pay for those services. If the attorney will bill against the advance payment for actual services performed, the advance is not a true retainer and is more properly characterized as either a security deposit or an advance payment of fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising clients or taking funds, practitioners must correctly label and treat payments: funds billed against are earned only as services are performed and are subject to refund rules; mischaracterizing an advance as an earned retainer can trigger disciplinary violation for failure to return unearned fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt refund of unearned advance fees (37 C.F.R. §10.40(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must promptly refund any part of a fee paid in advance that has not been earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to refund promptly is a violation. The order example: client paid $5,000 in advance, only $800 was earned by the registered patent attorney, and $4,200 remained unearned and had to be returned within the ordered timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt delivery/payment of client funds or property on request (37 C.F.R. §10.112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must promptly pay or deliver to the client, as requested by the client, the funds or other property in the practitioner's possession to which the client is entitled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays in returning client funds or property upon request constitute a disciplinary violation (mirrors the unearned-fee refund obligation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on charging/collecting illegal or clearly excessive fees (37 C.F.R. §10.36(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are proscribed from entering into an agreement for, charging, or collecting an illegal or clearly excessive fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of excessiveness apply to both total fees and hourly rates; the order found a $1,000/hour 'relationship attorney' rate and a $4,200 charge unreasonable under the circumstances. The 'practitioner of ordinary prudence' standard is applied to determine excessiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee division with non-partner/independent practitioner (37 C.F.R. §10.37(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing a fee for legal services with another practitioner who is not a partner in or associate of the practitioner's law firm or law office is prohibited unless (i) the client consents to employment of the other practitioner after a full disclosure that a division of fees will be made, (ii) the division is made in proportion to the services performed and responsibility assumed by each, and (iii) the total fee of the practitioners does not clearly exceed reasonable compensation for all legal services rendered to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure to the client and proportional division based on services/responsibility are required. The order cites a violation where the client did not consent after disclosure and the split was not proportional (initial $3,000/$2,000, later $800/$4,200).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of practitioner role, billing method, and termination-cost consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must communicate (verbally or in writing) the nature of his role (e.g., 'relationship attorney'), billing rates, and the consequences (e.g., hourly rate charges) if the client terminates the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to communicate such role/rate/termination billing terms can support findings of misconduct; in this case Respondent failed to communicate that his role would be as a 'relationship attorney' charged at $1,000/hour upon termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper accounting and return after partial performance or termination
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contracted practitioner or consultant performs part of the work and the client terminates the attorney-client relationship, fees must be allocated to reflect earned amounts and unearned amounts must be returned promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contracted registered patent attorney performed $800 worth of work, so the remainder of advance fees ($4,200) was unearned and required prompt return; returning only part and delaying return was a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness test standard for fees and rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the standard used in the order, 'a practitioner of ordinary prudence would be left with a definite and firm conviction' that a fee or hourly rate 'exceeds a reasonable fee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the applied legal test for determining whether a fee or rate is 'clearly excessive' under 37 C.F.R. §10.36(a); factual circumstances (scope of work, customary rates, services rendered) are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary history and respondent's recognition as mitigating/aggravating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors, such as no prior disciplinary history and the respondent's expressed understanding of why the conduct violated rules, are taken into account in determining sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order reduced punitive severity by noting the respondent's 32-year career without prior discipline and his apparent understanding, but still imposed a reprimand and return of funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, compliance deadlines, and enforcement process
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions ordered may include public reprimand, return of unearned fees within specified days (e.g., 60 days), submission of affidavit and corroborating documents of compliance (e.g., within 75 days), and consequences for noncompliance (Order to Show Cause, 15-day response period, potential suspension up to six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order prescribes concrete deadlines and procedures: OED may issue an Order to Show Cause, deliver materials to the USPTO Director, and request immediate suspension; returned checks/late payments constitute violation. The OED Director must comply with 37 C.F.R. §11.59 in enforcement procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication, redaction, and future use of disciplinary records
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall publish the Final Order in the Office of Enrollment and Discipline's electronic Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette (materially consistent with specified wording). The OED Director shall redact names and patent numbers as required for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The published record of the disciplinary proceeding may be considered in future complaints or proceedings as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations by the respondent; publication procedures and redaction obligations are part of the disciplinary process.
